sources.title: Tessl AI Native Dev ep 124 transcript (partial, ~1,800 words)
sources.note: Opening hook, intro, first exchange with Guy Podjarny (12-factor, spec-driven bet, dumb zone, Sean Grove). Cuts off mid-question at roughly minute 6-9 of 56. Episode itself not in inventory (inventory lists only Tessl ep 116, which does not involve Dex).

sources.title: Tessl ep 124 page: description, In this episode, chapter titles, write-up
sources.note: Third-party (Tessl) prose summary attributing positions to Dex; wording is paraphrase except short quoted fragments. Used for summarised cards.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we ran this for like 4 or 5 months before we realized, like, oh, this code base is actually unusable now
cards.claim: HumanLayer's 'read the plan, skip the code' pull-request experiment ran 4-5 months before the codebase proved unusable, with slower work and cross-file regressions.
cards.evidence_detail: First-person account of own team's experiment; no metrics given in the readable portion.
cards.landing: Self-reported or plan-only review is not a safe substitute for checking the code. Supports keeping the Opus reviewer per PR and not letting plan approval stand in for code review; the failure was slow and invisible for months, so FixFlow's phase-routine compliance needs an independent check.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The change over here cause a regression over here.
cards.claim: The unreviewed-code failure mode was non-local regressions, where a change in one place broke another, which a plan review cannot catch.
cards.evidence_detail: Own team's symptom description.
cards.landing: Argues for regression-catching verifiers and CI boundaries rather than plan fidelity alone; FixFlow has import-linter boundaries and CI, which is the right class of check.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we literally rebuilt the whole product from scratch
cards.claim: After the failed experiment the team rebuilt the product from scratch, and the co-founder hand-typed the new data architecture for the first two weeks.
cards.evidence_detail: Own team's story; Kyle typed 'every character by hand' in VS Code to plumb the data architecture.
cards.landing: Data architecture is the part a human should author directly. Relevant to FixFlow's Alembic-owned schema and the rule that models.py changes need deliberate migrations; do not delegate schema design to the agent.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We wanted to be living in the future.
cards.claim: Dex frames the YOLO pull-request bet as motivated by wanting to live in the future, a retrospective admission that the premise was an aspiration rather than evidence-based.
cards.evidence_detail: Opening hook; retrospective framing.
cards.landing: Cautionary framing for the owner: adopting autonomy levels ahead of evidence. No direct harness change.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the biggest change between summer of 2025 and now is actually like the planning metagame
cards.claim: The planning metagame has shifted: a plan file in mid-2025 was mainly a reliable way to make a model work longer and follow instructions, a role that has changed as models improved.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's retrospective reading of model behaviour; no measurement.
cards.landing: The justification for plans is time-dependent; FixFlow's phase routine should record why each plan artifact exists (resume, review, intent) so it can be retired when the reason lapses, and P1's cold-resume trial tests exactly the surviving reason.
cards.inventory_ref: Everything We Got Wrong About RPI (2026-03-24); AIE Miami 'Everything We got Wrong About RPI' 2026-04-20

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the first version of like first the compaction of intent
cards.claim: A plan file is a compaction of intent: a few hundred lines of markdown that stand in for every line of code, kept updated with what was done so work can resume from a clean context window.
cards.evidence_detail: Conceptual framing, no data.
cards.landing: Direct support for the draft-PR 'Plan @ sha' with decisions journal as a resume artifact; the cold-resume trial P1 is the test of whether it works as compacted intent.
cards.inventory_ref: A2 Advanced Context Engineering (frequent intentional compaction)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: keep that up to date with what was done, what changed
cards.claim: The plan file should be kept current with what was done and what changed so a later session can resume from a clean context.
cards.evidence_detail: Practice description.
cards.landing: The plan-as-journal needs maintenance every phase; with compliance self-reported (W2) this is the step most likely to be skipped, so a checkable close question (is the journal current) matters.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I coined the term called the dumb zone
cards.claim: The dumb zone: in mid-2025 results got markedly worse past roughly 100,000 tokens of context.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's experience-based threshold from July 2025; presented as a rough number, not a benchmark.
cards.landing: Supports one phase per session and a context budget; note the number is dated and he says it is higher now.
cards.inventory_ref: Latent Space 2026-03-06 (dumb zone, wrap up ~40%); Dev Interrupted 2026-02-17

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Obviously, that number is higher now.
cards.claim: The dumb-zone threshold has risen since mid-2025 but he believes a dumb zone still exists.
cards.evidence_detail: Qualitative statement; no new number given in the readable portion.
cards.landing: Do not hard-code the 100k figure into harness rules; treat the budget as a tunable setting and keep sessions phase-bounded rather than relying on a fixed token cap.
cards.inventory_ref: Long-Context Isn't the Answer (Kyle, 2026-03-23) shares the direction

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: too much focus is no focus
cards.claim: Too much information in context dilutes attention, so the human should deliberately choose what is in context and what is not.
cards.evidence_detail: Heuristic; no measurement offered.
cards.landing: Bears on the 390-line always-loaded CLAUDE.md: material that is not relevant to the current task competes for attention, which argues for trimming or conditional loading.
cards.inventory_ref: Getting Claude to Actually Read Your CLAUDE.md (2026-03-17); Writing a good CLAUDE.md (Kyle)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the spec will be the thing that is verifiable and executable
cards.claim: Dex relays Sean Grove's argument that the spec becomes the durable, compiled-from artifact and the conversation that produced code should be recorded rather than discarded.
cards.evidence_detail: Relaying another person's talk (Sean Grove, OpenAI); Dex endorsed it at the time and the page says he later found it insufficient.
cards.landing: Supports recording prompts and decisions with the PR (decisions journal) and saving workflows as artifacts (W5), while his later retraction warns not to treat the spec as a substitute for code review.
cards.inventory_ref: Thread 'Spec is the new code is not enough' 2026-03; wsff.md

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: throwing away the chat and shipping the code
cards.claim: Shipping code while discarding the prompts that produced it is like checking in the compiled jar and throwing away the source.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy relayed from Sean Grove.
cards.landing: Argues for persisting the chat-derived intent (plan, decisions journal, saved workflow scripts) alongside code; workflows authored per task and not saved (W5) are the 'thrown away' source.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude CLI is basically like the JVM of of agent coding
cards.claim: Claude Code's CLI has grown into a large-surface runtime with about 200 flags, whereas the Agent SDK at launch gave a small interface for small agent loops inside deterministic software.
cards.evidence_detail: Colour commentary; the 200-flags figure is an offhand estimate.
cards.landing: Agent loops embedded in deterministic code is the pattern behind FixFlow's Workflow-tool orchestration; little action beyond confirming direction.
cards.inventory_ref: A1 12-Factor Agents (deterministic code with LLM steps)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Strongly held, but pride out of your hands.
cards.claim: Dex says his opinions were strongly held but he is willing to change them when evidence shifts.
cards.evidence_detail: Self-description in the opening exchange; the transcript text is garbled (reads 'pride out of your hands').
cards.landing: Signals his earlier public advice (RPI, spec-is-code, lights-off) is dated; any card taken from 2025 material should be checked against his later retractions.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if you read the plan, the code is not as important
cards.claim: Engineers reviewed the plan in detail and let the agent implement it largely unsupervised, which was the YOLO pull-request experiment.
cards.evidence_detail: Page attributes the quoted line to Dex; same line appears in the transcript hook.
cards.landing: Warns that a plan-review gate without code or behaviour checks drifts; the harness's per-PR Opus refute-by-default reviewer is the counter.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: incredibly complex system
cards.claim: Letting models make architecture decisions with little human oversight produced an overcomplex system (desktop app, Go daemon over a Unix socket, agent sessions, MCP approval servers, SQLite) that nobody chose on purpose.
cards.evidence_detail: Page's description of Dex's own product history; attribution paraphrased.
cards.landing: Architecture and boundary decisions should stay human-owned; FixFlow's explicit slice boundaries and the rule that new import edges be added consciously fit this.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have to be smarter than you were
cards.claim: Old C-programming rule, as Dex cites it: debugging requires being smarter than when you wrote the code, so the system must stay simpler than your peak understanding of it.
cards.evidence_detail: Page paraphrases a rule Dex attributes to early C programming (Kernighan-style maxim); not measured. The quote is the page's gloss, not a verbatim Dex line.
cards.landing: A simplicity ceiling for agent-written code: if the owner cannot hold the design in their head, add review or simplify. Relevant to a single-owner codebase with 42 tables.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: back pressure
cards.claim: Better output comes from capturing intent up front and defining verifiers the agent can use to check its own work, not from reviewing code more carefully.
cards.evidence_detail: Page attributes the position and the term 'back pressure' to Dex; no data.
cards.landing: Direct support for L3: fast reliable verifiers (tests, lint, import-linter, mypy) are the main lever; invest in output-trimming wrappers and verifier speed.
cards.inventory_ref: Context-Efficient Backpressure (2025-12-09); AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: A model with a fast, reliable way to tell if it's on the right track
cards.claim: A model with a fast, reliable check that it is on the right track does dramatically better work.
cards.evidence_detail: Page's paraphrase of Dex; experience-based.
cards.landing: Prioritise verifier latency and signal quality (fast subset of CI the agent can run per change) over adding more reviewers.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: expected pain
cards.claim: Planning depth is a trade of expected pain: a two-sentence prompt is cheap with real rework odds, a five-hour handwritten spec costs more but leaves less to chance, and the right point depends on the cost of being wrong.
cards.evidence_detail: Chapter 'Planning as expected-pain management' (17:03) plus page prose; no figures beyond the illustrative examples.
cards.landing: Suggests scaling the phase routine by blast radius: money, lifecycle state machine and outbox changes get the full routine, copy or UI tweaks a light one, instead of one uniform routine.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: slider between determinism and adaptability
cards.claim: Specs are a slider between determinism and adaptability: how much of the outcome to dictate versus how much room the agent gets inside the frame.
cards.evidence_detail: Page attributes the framing to Dex; the page also poses it as a question to listeners.
cards.landing: A per-workflow setting worth recording in saved workflows (W5): tight scripts for invariants-heavy slices, looser for exploratory research.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: under 20%
cards.claim: On a university benchmark of extending a real codebase across sequential features (SlopCodeBench), leading results are still under 20%, so maintainable long-horizon coding has not improved as fast as the discourse implies.
cards.evidence_detail: Page cites a benchmark Dex references; leading strict pass rates under 20% match the 12-16% in his Oct 2026 report; Aug 2026 report showed 33% for two models, so the figure depends on model and date.
cards.landing: Do not expect agents to keep a codebase maintainable unattended; keep human architecture and review. Also a caution when comparing with the 33% figure from the August report.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: no fast oracle for maintainability
cards.claim: There is no fast oracle for maintainability, since a codebase's decay often shows only months later, which makes it hard to train or verify against.
cards.evidence_detail: Page paraphrase of Dex's argument; consistent with his wsff essay.
cards.landing: A verifier gap: tests catch behaviour but not decay. FixFlow needs a slow-loop check (periodic audit of boundaries, duplication, file growth) because per-PR checks will not show it.
cards.inventory_ref: wsff.md 2026-07-22 (test-passing rewards do not capture maintainability)

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: scheduled agents overnight
cards.claim: HumanLayer runs a handful of scheduled overnight agents, both deterministic checks and softer pattern-matching ones, that open PRs fixing small things before humans review new code.
cards.evidence_detail: Page describes it as HumanLayer's current practice; no counts or outcomes given.
cards.landing: A saved-workflow candidate: nightly janitor agents (lint drift, boundary violations, doc-vs-code drift such as the Alembic head number in CLAUDE.md) opening small PRs. FixFlow already has CI and a scheduler pattern but no such repo-maintenance agents.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: from your position, to your velocity
cards.claim: Dex's philosophy is to shift attention from the code in front of you (position) to the system that keeps producing good code (velocity).
cards.evidence_detail: Page paraphrase of a Dex line; framing, no data.
cards.landing: Argues investing in the harness itself (agents, skills, saved workflows) over per-task effort, which is W4 and W5.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: always be alpha in reviewing something
cards.claim: Dex does not think review disappears; he relays a dinner conversation that there will always be differentiating value in reviewing something, though not yet clear what.
cards.evidence_detail: Chapter 42:49 and page prose; hearsay of a conversation with an unnamed agent builder, adopted by Dex.
cards.landing: Keep a human review point; the six-question close and owner view are that point, so the open question is what the owner looks at (plan, behaviour, or code).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: whatever the model would have produced
cards.claim: Teams that skip review entirely tend to converge on whatever the model would produce for anyone asking the same question, with little differentiation.
cards.evidence_detail: Page paraphrase of Dex's view; no data.
cards.landing: Domain rules specific to FixFlow (invariants in CLAUDE.md, shop-specific behaviour) are exactly what unreviewed generation will not supply, so review is where they are enforced.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: software factories aren't like car factories
cards.claim: Chapter title says software factories differ from car factories, and the page says treating development as a factory changes how bugs compound; the argument itself is not in the readable text.
cards.evidence_detail: Chapter 37:59 title and one summary bullet only; content unread.
cards.landing: Placeholder: the content likely concerns defects compounding across generated work; needs the full transcript before use.

gaps: About 50 of 56 minutes are unread; the transcript ends mid-question around minute 6-9.
Likely covered by chapter 00:09:22 YOLO pull-request experiment: the detail of how the experiment was run, review rules, and how the failure was detected.
Chapter 00:11:09 Letting the model own the architecture: the desktop app / Go daemon / Unix socket / MCP approval / SQLite chain and why it was hard to undo; only the page summary is available.

Chapter 00:17:03 Planning as expected-pain management (about 11 minutes): likely the practical guidance on how much planning for which task, the two-sentence-prompt versus five-hour-spec tradeoff, and probably verifier design and back pressure.

Chapter 00:28:15 Slop Code Bench and the maintainability oracle problem (about 10 minutes): likely benchmark detail, why maintainability has no fast oracle, and possibly effort or model comparisons relevant to L1; none of this is readable.

Chapter 00:37:59 Why software factories aren't like car factories and the overnight agents: likely the substantive factory design, how bugs compound, what the scheduled agents check; only a one-line summary exists.
Chapter 00:42:49 'There will always be alpha in reviewing something' and the 12-month prediction about review advice: the close of the episode, only a paraphrase available.
The 12-factor-factories question raised by the host (Dex said 'I actually don't know') is unanswered in the readable text.
The page summary is Tessl's prose, so attributed positions are paraphrase; verbatim Dex wording is only in the transcript portion.
